Persistent Planar Memory for Video World Models

Yuze He Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Ant Group    Bin Tan Affiliation: Ant Group    Zelin Gao Affiliation: Ant Group Affiliation: HKUST    Yujun Shen Affiliation: Ant Group    Yong-Jin Liu ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Nan Xue Affiliation: Ant Group    Yinghao Xu Affiliation: Ant Group Affiliation: HKUST
Abstract

Video world models that generate and explore environments at scale need a persistent 3D memory of what they have produced. Plane primitives offer a natural candidate: a compact set of oriented planes captures the dominant structural elements (e.g., walls, floors, facades) of indoor and outdoor scenes, while requiring only 7 parameters per primitive. We present PPMem, a video world model that adopts plane primitives as its persistent 3D memory. PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer with a planar prediction head and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module: each autoregressive chunk jointly produces RGB video and planar geometry, which merges into a persistent plane memory that conditions subsequent chunks via rendered depth. The resulting memory is three orders of magnitude more compact than per-pixel point clouds (∼{\sim}100K primitives, ∼{\sim}5 MB for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross-view consistent (jointly predicted by the shared backbone), and adaptive (refined by the merging procedure as generation proceeds). On DL3DV and RealEstate10K, PPMem outperforms prior 3D-grounded world models in video quality while jointly producing metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry, sustaining coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes. Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/ppmem.

1 Introduction

Humans build the mental representation of their world through structural abstraction, decomposing scenes into points, lines, and planes. Among the three, planes carry disproportionate weight in human-made environments: walls, floors, ceilings, tabletops, building facades, and ground surfaces [2, 3] can all be approximated by only a small set of planes. A model that generates entire worlds, not just short clips, needs an analogous compact, structured memory of what it has produced. Plane primitives are a natural candidate for this role. Each primitive is parameterized by just 7 numbers (a center depth, two rectangular extents, and a rotation quaternion), which explicitly represents 3D geometric structure, and is orders of magnitude more compact than per-pixel representations. This raises a natural question: can plane primitives serve as a video world model’s representation, acting as a compact yet expressive persistent memory?

Video world modeling has emerged as a central frontier of AI, with systems that generate, simulate, and explore environments at scale. Existing approaches roughly fall into two camps. Pure-video world models, such as Genie 3 [6] and LingBot-world [5], train end-to-end on massive video corpora and rely on implicit attention and scale to maintain coherence. They achieve remarkable visual fidelity but expose no explicit 3D state for downstream conditioning, editing, or export. 3D-grounded video world models, the direct comparison group for PPMem, augment diffusion with explicit 3D geometric memory: a 2-frame point-cloud buffer (Gen3C [24]), an oriented-surfel store (VMem [13]), a TSDF volume paired with a keyframe pool (SPMem [36]), or a raw-frame retrieval bank (Context as Memory [41], WorldMem [38]). A related line, Voyager [11], jointly generates RGB and depth video and re-projects the generated depth into a point-cloud cache for conditioning subsequent chunks. Yet no existing 3D-grounded representation simultaneously exhibits the four properties that an explicit, persistent 3D state demands: compactness (orders of magnitude fewer primitives than dense representations), geometric explicitness (metric, rasterizable, exportable), cross-view consistency (jointly predicted by the generation backbone rather than assembled per frame), and adaptivity (refining the representation as generation proceeds).

We present PPMem, a video world model that uses plane primitives as its underlying 3D structure, accumulating them in a persistent plane memory for long-context video generation. Concretely, PPMem augments a video diffusion transformer (DiT) with two additions: a planar prediction head adapted from Plana3R [18] that regresses plane parameters per chunk, and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module that re-injects depth rendered from the memory into the DiT features. The memory plays a dual role: as the model’s structured 3D output (metric-scale depth, surface normals, and exportable planar geometry), and as persistent spatial conditioning for subsequent generation. Plane primitives are particularly well-suited for this role: after merging, ∼{\sim}100K planes cover a full scene three orders of magnitude more compactly than per-pixel point clouds (Table 1), and are fully differentiable through rectangular Gaussian rasterization [18]. Under large viewpoint changes, PPMem sustains coherent, metric-grounded video generation across hundreds of frames (Figure 1).

Compared with Gen3C, Voyager, VMem, and SPMem, PPMem achieves state-of-the-art video quality on DL3DV and RealEstate10K while accumulating under 10 MB of 3D memory.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We propose plane primitives as a 3D representation for video world models, accumulated in a persistent plane memory via cross-chunk geometric merging — to our knowledge, the first such memory that is simultaneously compact, geometrically explicit, cross-view consistent, and adaptive.

  • •

    We instantiate PPMem on a 5B Wan-2.2 DiT with a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module that re-injects rendered plane-pool depth into the generation process, enabling joint generation of RGB, metric depth, surface normals, and planar geometry in a single framework.

  • •

    We benchmark PPMem against Gen3C, Voyager, VMem, and SPMem on short-context and long-context evaluations across various datasets, demonstrating sustained visual and geometric coherence across hundreds of frames under large viewpoint changes.

2 Related Work

Camera-controlled video generation.

Recent video diffusion models with camera control [24, 1, 42, 7, 8, 35, 11] generate impressive short clips of 14–121 frames. However, extending generation to longer sequences reveals a representation gap: most methods either lack a persistent 3D state entirely (relying on camera embeddings or frame-level conditioning) or maintain only minimal geometric state. We organize prior work below by the level of 3D representation they maintain, highlighting a progressive trend toward more structured representations.

From depth maps to point clouds.

Depth estimation provides geometric cues for video world models [40]. At the simplest level, Gen3C [24] maintains a 2-frame point buffer (the seed frame and the most recent chunk-boundary frame, whose monocular depth is re-estimated and aligned to the cache at each autoregressive step); these 3D points are forward-warped as conditioning for the next generation chunk. This provides per-chunk geometric grounding but carries no persistent structure beyond two frames: all intermediate geometry is overwritten. Sora3R [22] predicts dense 4D pointmaps but is restricted to short sequences. At this level, depth and point representations are per-pixel and unstructured, offering no abstraction beyond raw geometry.

Surfels, TSDF, and frame-level memory.

A step up in structure, VMem [13] reconstructs oriented surfels via CUT3R [31] during autoregressive generation and uses them to index relevant past views; however, the surfel count grows with each generated frame. SPMem [36] builds a TSDF volume as spatial memory alongside an episodic keyframe pool; extending to long sequences requires re-estimating depth and re-integrating all accumulated frames into the volume at each step, with cost scaling linearly in sequence length. Context as Memory [41] retrieves raw past frames by FOV overlap, and WorldMem [38] uses cross-attention over a frame bank with relative Plücker embeddings; both operate at the frame level without maintaining explicit 3D geometry.

Joint depth and 3D generation.

A complementary line of work produces geometry alongside or from video. Voyager [11] jointly generates video and depth via shared diffusion and proposes re-projecting generated depth into a point-cloud cache for extended generation; its conditioning depth is normalized per-frame to relative disparity. IDCNet [21] outputs metric depth with camera control. GeometryCrafter [39] is a post-hoc tool that estimates temporally coherent point maps from existing video without generating new content. ViewCrafter [43] renders an externally estimated point cloud (DUSt3R [34]) at target viewpoints and uses diffusion to inpaint holes, consuming 3D rather than predicting it. FlashWorld [14] extends Wan 2.2 [29] with a 3D Gaussian decoder for joint multi-view generation, but repurposes the temporal dimension as a multi-view axis to produce static 3D scenes rather than temporal video sequences. None of these methods accumulate a compact, structured 3D representation that serves as persistent memory for long-context video generation.

Plane-based 3D reconstruction and our position.

Learning-based plane detection progresses from single-view segmentation (PlaneNet [20], PlaneRCNN [19], PlaneTR [27]) to differentiable multi-view reconstruction: AlphaTablets [9] optimizes alpha-composited planar primitives from monocular video, and PlanarSplatting [28] extends 3D Gaussian splatting [37] with planar constraints. Plana3R [18] performs feed-forward planar splatting via differentiable rectangular Gaussian rasterization, predicting metric-scale plane primitives from unposed image pairs in a single pass without per-scene optimization. All of these methods are reconstruction-only: they extract geometry from already-observed images. PPMem repurposes planar prediction as persistent spatial memory within a generative model: planes are jointly predicted alongside each generated video chunk by a shared diffusion backbone, and the accumulated plane pool feeds back as geometric conditioning for subsequent chunks. This bidirectional loop (generation →\to planes →\to conditioning →\to generation) has no counterpart in prior plane reconstruction work. We compare against alternative 3D representations in §3.1.

3 PPMem: Persistent Planar Memory

PPMem uses plane primitives as a compact, persistent 3D memory for autoregressive video generation. Unlike point clouds, surfels, or TSDF volumes used by prior 3D-grounded world models, plane primitives are predicted internally by the generation backbone (requiring no external depth estimator), yield cross-view consistent geometry by construction, and compress an entire scene into ∼{\sim}100K primitives — three orders of magnitude fewer than dense point clouds (Table 1). Each generated chunk jointly predicts video and a set of oriented rectangles in 3D, which are accumulated into a global pool via geometric merging; the pool is then rendered and fed back as depth conditioning for subsequent chunks. We describe the representation and memory mechanism (§3.1), the model architecture (§3.2), and training (§3.3) below.

3.1 Plane Primitives and Persistent Memory

A plane primitive in our framework is a parametric oriented rectangle in 3D space, defined by 7 parameters: a center depth zz along the camera ray (from which the 3D center 𝐱\mathbf{x} is derived via the camera intrinsics), two rectangular extents (sx,sy)(s_{x},s_{y}), and a rotation quaternion q∈ℝ4q\in\mathbb{R}^{4} whose third rotation-matrix column gives the surface normal 𝐧\mathbf{n}. Each primitive is rendered via differentiable rectangular Gaussian rasterization [18], producing depth and normal maps. At inference, predicted primitives are transformed to world coordinates and accumulated into the persistent plane pool, which after merging typically contains ∼{\sim}100K primitives (∼{\sim}5 MB) representing the full explored scene. Beyond compactness and internal predictability (Table 1), plane parameters can be merged across autoregressive steps via simple geometric criteria (occlusion voting, coplanarity, distance), making them well-suited as a cross-chunk memory.

Persistent plane pool.

The persistent plane pool 𝒫={𝐩1,𝐩2,…}\mathcal{P}=\{\mathbf{p}_{1},\mathbf{p}_{2},\ldots\} is a global, accumulating set of plane primitives across autoregressive chunks. After each chunk produces predicted planes 𝒫new\mathcal{P}_{\text{new}}, we merge them into 𝒫\mathcal{P} via the procedure below. Before the next chunk, we render 𝒫\mathcal{P} at the target camera poses and feed the rendered depth as conditioning to the generation model (detailed in §3.2). The full inference loop is summarized in Algorithm 1 (Appendix).

Plane pool maintenance.

After each chunk, new planes are merged into 𝒫\mathcal{P} with two goals: remove erroneous pool planes exposed by newer observations, and add new planes only where they contribute genuine new geometry. Each plane carries an observation quality score s=r/|cos⁡θ|s=r/|\cos\theta|, where rr is the Euclidean distance to the creating camera and θ\theta is the angle between the viewing ray and the surface normal (lower is better: the camera is closer and views the surface more perpendicularly). Three mechanisms maintain pool quality:

  1. 1.

    Occlusion deletion (correcting the past): pool planes that float in front of newly predicted surfaces are flagged via multi-camera voting and deleted.

  2. 2.

    Bidirectional quality dedup (improving the present): among nearby planes (within distance ϵ\epsilon), only the one with the better quality score survives — both within a chunk (intra-step, typically reducing count by ∼80%{\sim}80\%) and across chunks (cross-step).

  3. 3.

    Forward-looking prune (anticipating the future): pool planes that will be viewed from much closer in the next chunk (rnext/rcreated<τr_{\text{next}}/r_{\text{created}}<\tau) are removed proactively, as the upcoming chunk will produce higher-quality replacements. This uses only the next chunk’s camera poses, which are supplied as camera-control inputs rather than predicted.

Additional filtering stages are detailed in Algorithm 2 (Appendix). Surviving new planes are appended with metadata. Merging is local and does not require gradient-based optimization.

Pool-to-chunk conditioning.

Before each new chunk, we render 𝒫\mathcal{P} at the target camera poses via differentiable rasterization, producing partial depth maps that condition the next chunk through two complementary paths: VAE-encoded as a latent channel-concatenated with the noisy video input, and at pixel resolution through token-level fusion (§3.2). Unlike the fixed-size buffers of prior work, 𝒫\mathcal{P} accumulates geometry across all past chunks; its growth is controlled by merging, typically reaching ∼{\sim}100K primitives (∼{\sim}5 MB) after ∼{\sim}400 frames.

3.2 Model Architecture

PPMem builds on the Wan 2.2 video diffusion transformer [29] with two architectural additions (Figure 2): a plane prediction head that regresses plane primitives from DiT features, and a Depth Token Fusion (DTF) module that injects rendered plane-pool depth as token-level conditioning. At inference, PPMem generates video in ∼{\sim}25-frame chunks: target camera poses are used to project source views and render the plane pool into geometric conditioning (projected RGB, visibility masks, and depth maps), which are channel-concatenated with the noisy latent and fed to the DiT. The camera is encoded entirely through projected views rather than explicit parameters, decoupling the model from specific intrinsics or trajectory scales.

Plane prediction head.

The head, adapted from Plana3R [18], regresses the 7 plane parameters (§3.1) from DiT features. Since the DiT operates on a coarsely-patchified latent grid (H/16×W/16H/16\times W/16), we first apply a feature decoder that upsamples by 2×2{\times} in the spatial dimension. The decoder is initialized from the Wan 2.2 VAE decoder’s upsampling block, leveraging learned spatial priors [22]. Three small MLPs then regress center depth (in log-space over [0.2,277][0.2,277] m), rectangular extents (in metric units), and rotation quaternion at each feature location. The predicted primitives are rendered via differentiable rectangular Gaussian rasterization [18] and supervised against reconstructed metric depth (§3.3).

Depth token fusion (DTF).

To inject the plane pool’s geometric context into plane prediction, we use a DTF module (inspired by MDM [26]) in the geometry pass (§3.3). Partial depth maps rendered from 𝒫\mathcal{P} are tokenized via a 16×1616{\times}16 patch convolution and processed by a small ViT-Base encoder (∼{\sim}87 M parameters, ∼{\sim}1.7% of the 5B DiT), initialized from DINOv2-Base [23]; the encoded depth tokens are then concatenated with DiT feature tokens for fusion. Since rendered depth maps contain holes (unseen regions) and partially covered patches, we adopt a three-tier masking strategy before fusion: (i) fully invalid patches (zero coverage) are always dropped; (ii) mixed patches (partial coverage) are dropped with probability ρmix=0.75\rho_{\text{mix}}{=}0.75; (iii) fully valid patches are randomly dropped to reach a target overall mask ratio in [0.6,0.9][0.6,0.9]. This forces the DiT to remain robust to depth-conditioning sparsity while still benefiting from reliable conditioning signal.

3.3 Training

We train PPMem in two stages. Stage 1 fine-tunes the Wan 2.2 backbone for camera-controlled video generation, conditioning on projected source views and context frames with the standard flow-matching diffusion loss [17]. Stage 2 freezes the video backbone and attaches the plane prediction head, DTF module, and feature decoder; training proceeds exclusively with a geometry loss:

ℒ=λd​ℒdepth+λn​ℒnormal⏟per-patch+λdr​ℒdepthrend+λnr​ℒnormalrend⏟rasterization+λs​ℒsmooth,\mathcal{L}=\underbrace{\lambda_{d}\mathcal{L}_{\text{depth}}+\lambda_{n}\mathcal{L}_{\text{normal}}}_{\text{per-patch}}+\underbrace{\lambda_{d}^{r}\mathcal{L}_{\text{depth}}^{\text{rend}}+\lambda_{n}^{r}\mathcal{L}_{\text{normal}}^{\text{rend}}}_{\text{rasterization}}+\lambda_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}, (1)

where the per-patch terms supervise depth (L1L_{1}, log-space) and normals (cosine + L1L_{1}) per spatial token, the rasterization terms compare rendered planes against ground truth (enabled after 1000 warmup iterations), and ℒsmooth\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}} is a total-variation regularizer on rendered depth. Default weights: λd=0.2\lambda_{d}{=}0.2, λn=0.05\lambda_{n}{=}0.05, λdr=0.02\lambda_{d}^{r}{=}0.02, λnr=0.01\lambda_{n}^{r}{=}0.01, λs=0.02\lambda_{s}{=}0.02 (full configuration in Appendix A.2). We inject LoRA adapters [10] on self-attention in all 30 DiT blocks, providing geometry-specific attention patterns atop the frozen video-generation weights. At inference, video and geometry are fully decoupled: all denoising steps run with the frozen Stage-1 backbone (LoRA disabled), producing video at the original model’s quality. A single additional forward pass with LoRA enabled extracts plane geometry from the final-step features. Stage 1 runs for ∼{\sim}7 000 iterations and Stage 2 for ∼{\sim}5 000.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Training data. We train on a mixture of DL3DV [16] and RealEstate10K [44] (80K+ clips) at 576×1024576{\times}1024 resolution. For ablation experiments (Tables 3–5), we train on a DL3DV indoor subset (∼{\sim}5K clips) at 288×512288{\times}512. Both settings use metric depth from MoGe-2 [33], scale-aligned to VGGT [30] reconstructions (Appendix A.1).

Test sets. We evaluate on 100 DL3DV test scenes and 100 RealEstate10K (RE10K) clips (both disjoint from training); ablations use the DL3DV indoor subset (56 scenes). For long-context evaluation, we use the full DL3DV test sequences (300–400 frames each), which exhibit substantially larger camera motion than RE10K and stress the persistent memory mechanism.

Baselines. We compare against Gen3C [24], Voyager [11], VMem [13], and SPMem [36], all run with their public release code and default hyperparameters. All methods receive ground-truth camera trajectories and first-frame depth (or Plücker rays for VMem).

Protocol. Each method generates at its own native resolution and aspect ratio; input images and ground truth are center-cropped and resized to match, so that metrics reflect each method’s best operating point. We report short-range results at N=49N{=}49 and N=121N{=}121 frames (Table 2).

Metrics. For short-range evaluation (Table 2), we report PSNR, LPIPS, CLIP similarity, and DINOv2 similarity. For long-context evaluation (Figure 3), we report CLIP and DINOv2 similarity as a function of frame index, which capture semantic and structural fidelity across large viewpoint changes. Per-frame depth accuracy against baselines is shown in Figure 5(a); depth metrics — absolute relative error (AbsRel =|d−d∗|/d∗=|d-d^{*}|/d^{*}), threshold accuracy (δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25), and mean normal angle error (Normal∘) — are additionally reported in the ablation tables.

Implementation. PPMem is built on Wan 2.2 TI2V 5B [29]. We use a per-frame VAE encoder (no temporal compression, 1:1 latent-to-frame mapping) to preserve per-frame geometric correspondence for plane prediction. Depth conditioning is log-normalized over [0.2,99][0.2,99] m, while the plane head predicts log-depth over [0.2,277][0.2,277] m. We train with learning rate 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5}, classifier-free guidance dropout 0.1, and context-block dropout 0.1 (all context frames dropped together). Full hyperparameters are in Appendix Table S1.

4.2 Short-Range Comparison

Table 2 reports short-range video quality on DL3DV and RealEstate10K. PPMem achieves the best results across all metrics on both datasets and both frame budgets, despite using a smaller base model (Wan 2.2 5B) compared to Gen3C (Cosmos 7B) and Voyager (HunyuanVideo ∼{\sim}13B). Table 2 compares complete systems; Table 3 isolates the memory mechanism by swapping it on the same Wan 2.2 generator.

Beyond video quality, PPMem jointly outputs metric-scale depth. Figure 5(a) compares per-frame depth accuracy against Voyager — the only other baseline with joint depth output — over 121 frames on DL3DV. PPMem maintains lower AbsRel and higher δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 accuracy than Voyager.

4.3 Long-Context Generation under Large Viewpoint Change

We evaluate all methods on the full DL3DV test sequences (300–400 frames each), where large camera motion across many autoregressive chunks tests each method’s ability to maintain coherent generation far from the initial viewpoint. Figure 3 plots CLIP and DINOv2 similarity against frame index: PPMem maintains the highest perceptual fidelity throughout, with the gap widening over time — most dramatically on DINOv2, where PPMem leads the next-best method by ∼{\sim}0.27 at frame 300. Figure 4 shows a representative example: PPMem preserves scene structure and color consistency across the full sequence, while all baselines degrade visibly as the viewpoint diverges.

4.4 Ablations

We ablate four design aspects below. All variants are trained on the DL3DV indoor subset at 288×512288{\times}512, evaluated on the 56-scene indoor test split over 3 autoregressive chunks, and share the same Stage-1 backbone and Stage-2 training recipe. Additional ablation studies on context frame composition and plane pool merging stages are in Appendix B.

3D representation and prediction (Table 3).

To validate the choice of plane primitives and joint prediction, we compare three alternative configurations at inference time (no retraining): (i) Without persistent memory: a same-model rollout using the model’s own predicted depth but no persistent memory. (ii) Point cloud memory: we replace the plane pool with a Gen3C-style mechanism — MoGe-2 [33] estimates per-frame monocular depth on each generated frame, and the resulting point cloud conditions the next chunk via forward warping. (iii) Post-hoc Plana3R: instead of using the joint plane prediction head, we run a standalone pretrained Plana3R model [18] on each generated frame post-hoc and accumulate the resulting planes into the pool. Our joint plane pool outperforms all three alternatives, with particularly large gains on depth (δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25: 70.370.3 vs 64.064.0/55.055.0/57.057.0), indicating that the persistent memory contributes primarily to geometric consistency and long-horizon stability.

Depth conditioning mechanism (Table 4).

The dominant effect is the presence of depth conditioning itself: without it, depth accuracy collapses (AbsRel 0.4360.436, δ<1.25=30.7%\delta{<}1.25=30.7\%) and video quality also degrades (PSNR 14.1914.19 vs 14.9114.91). The video improvement is indirect: better depth prediction yields a higher-quality plane pool, which in turn provides better projected conditioning (RGB, masks, rendered depth) for subsequent chunks — a cascading benefit across autoregressive steps. Given depth, channel concatenation and DTF perform comparably on the ablation benchmark, where training and evaluation both use well-aligned metric depth. At inference, the depth conditioning comes from plane pool rendering, which introduces holes, partial coverage, and scale imperfections. Figure 5(b) tests this via a scale faithfulness probe (whether predicted depth scales proportionally when the input depth conditioning is rescaled) — we deliberately multiply the input depth by a known factor and measure the predicted/GT depth ratio. DTF tracks input scale faithfully (1.00±0.011.00\pm 0.01 at scale 1.0), while channel concatenation exhibits a compressed response at extreme scales, suggesting that the VAE bottleneck discards fine-grained scale information. DTF’s token-level fusion with explicit validity masking is better suited to the imperfect conditioning encountered during autoregressive inference. The two base variants are trained exclusively on well-aligned metric depth (scale ≈ 1{\approx}\,1). We additionally train both fusion schemes with per-video depth scale augmentation (s∼logU⁡[0.25,4]s\sim\mathrm{logU}[0.25,4]), and find that it substantially improves scale faithfulness in both cases, with DTF + scale augmentation tracking the input scale most closely overall (natural-log RMSE to the identity mapping: 0.1310.131, vs. 0.2730.273 for DTF alone and 0.2930.293 for concatenation with the same augmentation).

Feature decoder and loss components (Table 5).

Replacing the original Plana3R upsampling head [18] with a VAE-initialized decoder improves δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 by +11.1+11.1 pp (59.2→70.359.2\to 70.3) and AbsRel by −0.046-0.046 (0.256→0.2100.256\to 0.210), showing that the video VAE’s learned spatial prior meaningfully benefits geometric prediction. For loss components, removing the rasterization loss degrades δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 by −3.9-3.9 pp and Normal∘ by +1.2∘+1.2^{\circ}; removing the normal loss causes depth to collapse entirely (all-zero output), confirming it is critical for learning the coupled depth-normal parameterization.

5 Conclusion

We presented PPMem, a video world model that uses plane primitives as persistent 3D memory for long-context generation. The plane pool satisfies the four properties we identified for cross-chunk memory: it is compact (∼{\sim}100K primitives for a full scene), geometrically explicit (metric depth, normals, exportable surfaces), cross-view consistent (jointly predicted by the generation backbone), and adaptive (refined via geometric merging as generation proceeds). Experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that PPMem sustains both video quality and depth accuracy under large viewpoint changes, outperforming Gen3C, Voyager, VMem, and SPMem.

Limitations and future work.

PPMem is best suited for structured scenes where planar primitives are a good geometric prior. A quantitative breakdown of performance versus scene planarity is provided in Appendix B.3. For highly organic environments (dense vegetation, water) the representation may capture less detail than point-based alternatives. Extreme camera trajectories not seen during training can also degrade quality. Our two-stage design deliberately freezes the pretrained video backbone and trains geometry through lightweight adapters, which preserves the backbone’s generation quality but forgoes end-to-end co-adaptation of the video and geometry objectives; jointly optimizing both is a more general alternative we leave to future work. Extending to dynamic plane primitives and scaling to open-world scenes are natural next steps. Like all video generation models, PPMem could potentially be misused for synthetic media creation.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Dataset Preprocessing

Training data.

For ablation experiments (Tables 3–5 and Tables S2–S3), we use 5K preprocessed DL3DV [16] indoor video clips at 𝟐𝟖𝟖×𝟓𝟏𝟐\mathbf{288{\times}512} resolution. For the final model, we train on a mixture of DL3DV and RealEstate10K [44] (80K+ clips) at 𝟓𝟕𝟔×𝟏𝟎𝟐𝟒\mathbf{576{\times}1024} resolution. Each clip is paired with per-frame metric depth, surface normals, and camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Dense monocular depth and normals are estimated by MoGe-2 [33] and aligned to multi-view reconstruction from VGGT [30] via per-frame scale fitting; the median scale is applied globally to place all depths and camera translations in a consistent metric coordinate system.

Offline conditioning pipeline.

A central design principle of PPMem is that all training conditioning is generated by the same plane-based rendering process used at inference, so that the model trains on realistic imperfections (holes, depth discontinuities, partial coverage) rather than perfect ground-truth projections. Concretely, we run an offline incremental plane reconstruction pipeline [28, 12] on each video clip to produce all conditioning signals:

  1. 1.

    Incremental reconstruction. Frames are partitioned into segments of 24. Each segment undergoes plane-based reconstruction (optimizing plane primitives to fit the aligned metric depth). After each segment, new planes are merged with the accumulated pool and jointly optimized across all frames observed so far.

  2. 2.

    Conditioning generation. After processing segment kk, we render the accumulated plane pool at the next segment’s cameras (segment k+1k{+}1), producing partial depth maps that serve as the depth conditioning for that segment’s training sample. This one-step look-ahead mirrors the inference-time loop, where each chunk’s depth conditioning comes from rendering the pool accumulated from all previous chunks. Two source views are also selected from all preceding segments’ frames via greedy union-coverage maximization and forward-warped to each target camera, producing projected RGB images and soft visibility masks (continuous values in [0,1][0,1] from bilinear splatting weights).

  3. 3.

    Context frame selection. Overlap frames are selected from all preceding segments via greedy union-coverage maximization over the current segment’s target cameras. These are actual video frames (not rendered views); their accompanying depth comes from the accumulated plane pool render at those cameras.

Because the conditioning is rendered from the same plane-based reconstruction used at inference, it naturally exhibits the same artifact distribution: holes in unseen regions, depth edges at object boundaries, partial coverage from oblique viewpoints, and planar approximation errors. The gap between training and autoregressive inference thus reduces to the difference in plane quality (offline reconstruction vs. online model predictions), rather than a distribution shift between perfect ground truth and imperfect model outputs.

Context frames.

For each training segment, three types of context frames are prepended along the temporal dimension:

  • •

    Anchor: frame 0 of the video, providing a long-range identity anchor.

  • •

    History: real RGB frames stratified-randomly sampled from preceding segments, each accompanied by depth rendered from the accumulated plane pool.

  • •

    Overlap: real RGB frames selected by greedy union-coverage maximization (as described above), with plane-pool-rendered depth.

Each context type is assigned a distinct negative RoPE temporal index, encoding it as temporally prior to the generated sequence. Context dropout is applied with probability 0.1 during training (the entire context block is dropped), encouraging robustness to partial or absent context at inference. We ablate the contribution of each context type in Table S2.

DiT input assembly.

The DiT receives conditioning through three complementary pathways:

Channel concatenation. All RGB, mask, and depth signals are VAE-encoded using the Wan 2.2 separate VAE (1:1 frame mapping, zdim=48z_{\text{dim}}{=}48). Six such latents are concatenated along the channel dimension: the noisy video latent, two projected source-view RGB latents, two projected visibility-mask latents, and the depth conditioning latent, yielding 6×48=2886{\times}48=288 input channels in total.

Temporal prepend. Context frames (anchor, history, overlap) are prepended as clean tokens (timestep = 0{=}\,0) before the main frames along the temporal dimension, providing the model with real observed frames as conditioning memory.

Token-level fusion. The same depth map also enters the model at pixel resolution through the DTF module (§3.2), providing fine-grained geometric awareness via self-attention between depth tokens and DiT feature tokens.

A.2 Training Hyperparameters

Plane head initialization.

Each of the three prediction MLPs (center depth, rectangular extents, rotation quaternion) is initialized so that the last layer produces a stable constant output before training begins: depth bias is set to 2.0 m with zero weights, radii bias to 0.1 m with zero weights, and rotation bias to the identity quaternion [1,0,0,0][1,0,0,0] with near-zero weights (σ=0.001\sigma{=}0.001). During the rasterization-loss warmup (first 1000 iterations), depth and normals are supervised by per-patch losses; the extents receive no direct gradient but remain at their initialized constant, ensuring stable rasterization once the rendering loss is enabled.

A.3 Inference Setup

PPMem generates video autoregressively in 25-frame chunks; the last frame of each chunk is reused as the first frame of the next. Given an input image, a text prompt, and a target camera trajectory, the full pipeline proceeds as follows.

Initial chunk (chunk 0).

The input image is used as the first frame. An initial depth estimate (from any monocular depth estimator or ground-truth depth, if available) is projected to the remaining 24 target cameras to produce partial RGB images and visibility masks (the single input frame is used as both source views to match the two-view conditioning format). The initial depth also serves as the depth conditioning signal for DTF. The DiT then generates the first 25-frame video clip following the same two-pass generation procedure described below (50 denoising steps with the frozen backbone, then one geometry LoRA pass); the predicted plane primitives initialize the plane pool.

Subsequent chunks (chunk k≥1k\geq 1).

Each subsequent chunk follows a three-phase pipeline:

  1. 1.

    Conditioning: the cumulative plane pool is rendered at the next chunk’s target cameras via rectangular Gaussian rasterization, producing partial depth maps. Two source views are selected from the pool’s accumulated frames (greedy coverage maximization) and projected to the target cameras. Context frames — an anchor frame (frame 0 of the video), up to 5 history frames from preceding chunks, and coverage-sorted overlap frames — are prepended along the temporal dimension.

  2. 2.

    Generation and plane prediction: the DiT performs 50 denoising steps with classifier-free guidance scale 5.0, producing the generated video. We then re-run the final denoising step with the Stage 2 LoRA adapters enabled: this additional forward pass provides geometry-adapted DiT features to the plane prediction head, which regresses plane primitives. The 50-step video generation uses only the frozen Stage 1 backbone, preserving video quality; the extra LoRA step serves solely to produce plane predictions. Each predicted plane is transformed from camera space to world space using the known camera extrinsics.

  3. 3.

    Pool update: the predicted planes are merged into the cumulative pool via the merging pipeline (Algorithm 2), which removes floaters, deduplicates redundant planes, and prunes planes that will be better observed by the next chunk.

Output.

After all chunks are generated, PPMem produces: (a) the full generated video, (b) per-frame metric-scale depth and surface normal maps (from the plane prediction head), and (c) the cumulative plane pool as a compact 3D reconstruction of the generated scene (exportable as a mesh via triangulation of the rectangular primitives).

Compute overhead.

The plane pool adds negligible cost relative to video denoising. At 576×1024576{\times}1024, denoising dominates each chunk (∼{\sim}128 s); pool rasterization (∼{\sim}1.7 s for 25 views) and merging (∼{\sim}0.3 s) are two orders of magnitude cheaper.

End-to-end memory accounting.

We account separately for scene-growing, bounded per-chunk, and fixed model state. At a long-rollout snapshot, our persistent pool (106K planes, 4.8 MiB including merger metadata) is substantially smaller than a matched point-cloud variant that accumulates per-pixel 3D points over the same rollout and resolution (1.7 GiB). Context frames, projected views, rendered depth, and merge buffers remain bounded per chunk, with a maximum simultaneous non-model state of 41 MiB, including the plane pool. DTF, the geometry decoder/head, and geometry LoRA add 1.1 GiB of fixed BF16 model state; no separate acceleration structure is used.

A.4 Plane Pool Merging Algorithm

Algorithm 2 details the full merging pipeline. Each plane carries an observation quality score s=r/|cos⁡θ|s=r/|\cos\theta| (defined in main paper §3.1), where rr is the Euclidean distance to the creating camera and θ\theta is the angle between the viewing ray and the surface normal. A lower score means the plane was observed from a closer, more frontal viewpoint and is therefore more reliable. This score drives the quality comparisons in stages 3, 5, and 6.

Default thresholds: δocc=0.1\delta_{\text{occ}}{=}0.1 (10% relative margin), θe=1.0\theta_{e}{=}1.0 (Sobel on log-depth), ϵsame=0.5\epsilon_{\text{same}}{=}0.5 m, dmax=5d_{\max}{=}5 m, ρ=0.2\rho{=}0.2 (20% camera agreement), τ=0.3\tau{=}0.3.

We ablate the contribution of each stage in Table S3 (Section B.2).

Appendix B Additional Ablations and Comparisons

B.1 Context Configurations

Table S2 ablates the three types of context frames that condition each autoregressive chunk: (i) overlap: past RGB frames selected by coverage of the target viewpoints; (ii) history frames from preceding chunks; and (iii) an anchor frame (frame 0 of the video). All configurations are evaluated at inference time without retraining, leveraging the 10% context dropout applied during training.

Component ablation (top).

Removing all context degrades δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 from 70.3 to 64.2. Overlap frames alone recover most of this gap (++5.0 pp) and achieve the lowest AbsRel (0.208). Adding history and anchor further improves PSNR and perceptual metrics, with the full combination achieving the best balance across all metrics.

History scaling (bottom).

Increasing the number of history frames beyond the default (5) yields only marginal gains (PSNR 14.91 →\to 14.94) while prefix sequence length and attention cost grow with the history count. We keep 5 as the default for this quality/compute tradeoff.

B.2 Plane Pool Merging Phase Ablation

Table S3 cumulatively adds merging mechanisms to the baseline. Within-chunk dedup (stage 3) provides the largest single improvement, reducing per-chunk plane count by ∼{\sim}4.5×\times (518K →\to 116K) while improving δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 on both indoor and outdoor scenes. Every subsequent addition further improves δ<1.25\delta{<}1.25 monotonically on both splits. Boundary rejection uses a single global threshold shared across indoor and outdoor scenes, trading a small amount of coverage for stricter geometry filtering.

Accumulated plane pool.

We render each final pool over the complete generated trajectory. Across 56 scenes, the accumulated pool compresses the per-chunk plane predictions into only ∼{\sim}100K planes while retaining accuracy close to them (0.241 vs. 0.210 AbsRel), with 98.7% image coverage. Figure S1 compares the pool against Plana3R reconstructions of the same generated videos.

B.3 Scene Planarity

We compute scene planarity independently of PPMem predictions. For every view in the reference sequence, we use estimated depth and surface normals to group neighboring valid pixels satisfying surface-normal and local 3D plane-consistency constraints. Scene planarity is the fraction of valid-depth pixels, pooled across views, covered by connected planar regions of at least 256 pixels. Across the 100 DL3DV scenes, planar coverage has a Spearman correlation of 0.33 with PSNR at 121 frames. Table S4 groups the scenes into within-domain tertiles of planar coverage.

Overall, lower planarity is associated with a gradual decrease in PSNR and depth accuracy, while LPIPS varies only mildly across the three groups.

B.4 Comparison to Non-3D-Persistent Baselines

We additionally evaluate WorldPlay [25] and MemCam [4], which use historical-frame context without an explicit persistent 3D representation, on the same DL3DV evaluation set (Table S5).

Appendix C Additional Qualitative Results

Figures S4 and S4 compare long-context generation on DL3DV outdoor rooftop and indoor store scenes. Figure S2 shows degradation of fine text under zoom-in.
